PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deployment regime is night, fixed-brightness near-IR illumination, fixed camera pose 7 m down the pinch point, 50 mm f/4 ISO 190 1/500 s, focused at ~3.5 m, 30 s revisit. The training regime is GBIF multimedia: daylight, visible RGB, arbitrary viewpoint, background, lighting and exposure.

Dominant domain shift is spectral/illumination and fixed-viewpoint/background. Deployment images are effectively monochrome IR with essentially constant photometry. Brightness A/B/C, non-linear tone-curve C, colour noise J, salt-and-pepper K, RGB channel swizzle I all stay in RGB colour space and keep the network able to use colour cues that are absent at test time. With fixed IR illumination brightness jitter is a variation that does not exist at deployment and will encourage invariance to a non-existent nuisance.

Geometry is essentially fixed. Scale D is set by the 7 m baseline and 50 mm focal length; the only real scale variation is the small depth change along the 7 m corridor. The chosen 1/500 s exposure makes classic directional motion blur H negligible for terrestrial mammals; motion ≈ cm per exposure. Vertical flip E is biologically impossible. Horizontal flip F is the only spatial symmetry that is physically plausible in principle – animals can transit left-to-right vs right-to-left – but it mirrors the fixed, non-symmetric rock background and does not address the colour→IR, day→night shift. Most colleagues note it is at best a marginal, least-harmful regulariser.

Depth of field is limited. With f=50 mm, N=4, focus ≈3.5 m hyperfocal ≈31 m on full frame, near≈3.14 m far≈3.93 m, DOF≈0.8 m; on a small sensor DOF is even smaller. Animals in front of/behind the mid-plane will be defocused in deployment whereas GBIF images are sharp. Gaussian blur G is the only augmentation that simulates a real optics effect present at deployment. The specified 11×11 σ=3 kernel is a strong, uniform blur and not a distance-dependent defocus model, and colour/brightness/scale/motion augmentations add variation that is absent in the fixed rig.

Thus no listed operation closes the colour daylight → monochrome IR, variable background → fixed rock corridor domain gap. In a strict sense the useful operation would be grayscale/IR conversion of the training set and matching the fixed photometry, which is not offered. Among the menu, colour/brightness/scale/noise/blur augmentations either simulate non-existent variation or keep colour dependence; horizontal flip is the least harmful geometric symmetry. The consensus split is between L none improves / is counterproductive and F horizontal flip as the least harmful plausible augmentation; G Gaussian blur is defended as the only optics-related effect that is systematically present off the focus plane. Unresolved is how severe the rock-background asymmetry makes a horizontal mirror unrealistic in practice. My current belief is that strictly none of A-K materially closes the GBIF→IR trap gap, with horizontal flip being the only physically admissible transform in the list and Gaussian defocus the only optics effect that could help, but neither addresses the dominant spectral/domain shift.

12.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The train / test gap is not generic natural-image variation.

* Deployment is a single fixed rig: camera bolted at one rock face looking 7 m to the opposite rock, 50 mm focal length, focused at ~3.5 m, ISO 190, f/4.0, 1/500 s, one frame every 30 s, 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise under a fixed-brightness near-IR illuminator. Images are therefore effectively monochrome / IR, constant photometry, constant viewpoint, fixed background of the two rocks, and essentially fixed exposure / noise. Scale in the image is set by species size and the small depth range of the pinch point.

* Training is several thousand GBIF multimedia images per class: daylight, visible-spectrum colour, arbitrary viewpoint, background, illumination and sensor. The dominant domain shift is spectral / colour → monochrome IR, day → night, variable background → fixed rock corridor, variable viewpoint → fixed 7 m pinch point.

Photometric augmentations A,B,C,I,J,K
- Linear / non-linear brightness A,B,C on RGB or luminance and colour noise J, salt-and-pepper K add variation that is essentially absent at deployment because the IR illuminator + fixed ISO/f/stop/exposure locks brightness. They keep colour information in the training set and encourage reliance on colour cues that are absent at test.
- RGB channel swizzle I is the only listed operation that attacks colour dependence. It destroys a consistent R→R,G→G,B→B mapping and pushes the network toward luminance / texture cues, but it still lives in RGB and does not simulate a monochromatic IR image. Colleagues 3 and 8 argue it is the closest proxy to the needed colour→IR invariance; colleagues 1,4,11,12 argue it still keeps colour in the loop and does not bridge the spectral gap.

Geometric / acquisition augmentations
- Scale D: image scale is essentially fixed by the 7 m baseline and 50 mm lens, with only a modest depth-dependent change. Adding arbitrary scale creates variation that will not occur.
- Vertical flip E is biologically/physically impossible for a ground mammal in a ground-level ravine.
- Horizontal flip F: an animal can transit the pinch point left-to-right or right-to-left. A left-right mirror is a physically plausible deployment variation for a corridor camera and is the standard camera-trap invariance. It does not address the colour→IR shift and it mirrors the fixed rock background, but it is the only colour-agnostic transform that does not introduce unphysical photometry. Colleagues 2,6,7,12,15 favor F as the least harmful / most realistic of the list.
- Gaussian blur G 11×11 σ=3: the rig has a finite depth of field. At ~50 mm f/4 focus 3.5 m hyperfocal ~20.8 m gives near ≈2.5 m far ≈4.9 m, so animals in front of/behind the plane of focus will be defocused. GBIF images are sharp. Colleagues 5,10,5 argue defocus simulation is the only real image-formation mismatch not covered by the fixed illumination and is important; critics note the 11×11 σ=3 kernel is strong and the DOF still covers most of the usable corridor, and blur does not address the colour→IR gap.
- Motion blur H: 1/500 s is ~2 ms. Even at several m/s the in-exposure translation is centimetres, and with the short exposure and moderate magnification it is negligible. Colleagues 13,14 argue motion is the main mismatch because GBIF is static; colleagues 2,6,12 argue the shutter makes directional motion blur unrealistic.
- Noise K,J: ISO 190, short exposure and fixed IR source give low sensor noise; synthetic colour / salt-and-pepper noise does not match the deployment statistics.

Overall assessment
Strictly speaking the colour/daylight → fixed-brightness monochrome IR, fixed-view fixed-background shift is not closed by any A-K operation. The useful simulation would be grayscale/IR conversion and freezing photometry, which is not listed. In that strict sense L, none of the above, is correct and most listed augmentations will add field-inconsistent variation and can degrade performance.

If forced to pick the least harmful / most deployment-relevant operation among the menu, the discussion splits between:
- F horizontal mirror as the only physically plausible geometric symmetry that increases pose coverage without adding colour/photometric variation;
- G Gaussian defocus as a proxy for the finite DOF that will be present for animals off the 3.5 m focus plane;
- I channel swizzle as the best attempt to reduce colour dependence toward an IR-like luminance cue.

Unresolved tension remains between the dominant colour→IR domain shift that no listed augmentation addresses and the secondary geometric/ optical effects of limited DOF and left-right transit direction.

reflection_text.5:
The deployment distribution is strongly constrained and very different from the GBIF training distribution.

Deployment:
* Night only, 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, fixed-brightness near-IR illumination. Images are effectively monochrome / luminance only, constant photometry.
* Fixed rig: camera at face of one rock facing the other 7 m away, 50 mm focal length, focused at mid-point ~3.5 m, ISO 190, f/4.0, 1/500 s. Camera pose, background = two rocks/ravine, illumination level and exposure are fixed.
* Scale is essentially fixed by the 7 m baseline and 50 mm focal length; small residual variation only from depth around the focus plane and species size. 1/500 s makes motion blur negligible for terrestrial mammals. Depth of field at 50 mm f/4 ~ ~1-4 m around the focus plane, so some defocus for animals off the mid-plane is expected.

Training:
* Several thousand GBIF multimedia images per species, colour daylight, arbitrary viewpoint, background, illumination, scale.

Dominant domain shift = colour daylight variable background → monochrome fixed-brightness IR fixed-viewpoint fixed-background. No listed augmentation implements a true grey-scale/IR conversion.

Photometric augmentations A,B,C,I,J,K:
* A linear brightness multiply on RGB, B on luminance, C non-linear tone-curve, I RGB channel swizzle, J colour noise, K salt-and-pepper.
* Under fixed IR illumination brightness is constant and colour is absent. These keep colour information in training and introduce variation that does not exist at test time. Colleagues 1,2,4,6,11,12 argue they are counter-productive / irrelevant. Colleague 3/8 argue channel swizzle I is the closest to forcing colour-invariance and relying on luminance structure, i.e. the best attack on the colour→IR gap among the list.

Geometric / blur:
* Scale D: Fixed geometry makes scale largely fixed. Some colleagues argue scale augmentation would only teach tolerance to scales that never occur; others note small depth-induced scale change at entrance vs focus plane.
* Vertical flip E: universally deemed physically impossible for ground mammals in this corridor.
* Horizontal flip F: animals can transit left-to-right or right-to-left through the pinch point; a left-right mirror is a physically plausible deployment variation. Colleagues 2,6,7,12,15 argue this is the only physically admissible, distribution-preserving augmentation and the standard camera-trap invariance. Colleague 11 notes it still mirrors a fixed non-symmetric rock background.
* Gaussian blur G 11x11 σ=3: Colleagues 5,10 argue the dominant real image-formation mismatch is limited depth of field; defocus off the 3.5 m plane is systematic and a Gaussian blur can simulate it. Colleagues 2,4,6,7 argue the chosen kernel is too strong and colour/day→IR shift dominates.
* Motion blur H: Colleagues 13,14 argue directional motion smear will be present; colleagues 2,4,6,12 argue 1/500 s exposure makes motion blur negligible ≈ cm movement.

Consensus points:
* Colour/brightness jitter does not bridge day colour → night IR; fixed illumination means brightness variation is spurious.
* Motion blur is unlikely at 1/500 s; vertical flip is implausible.
* Real improvement would require IR/greyscale training data or domain adaptation, which is not listed.

Disagreement remains on the least-worst listed augmentation:
* L – None improves deployment accuracy, all listed augmentations are neutral/harmful.
* F – Horizontal flip is the only physically plausible geometric regulariser.
* G – Gaussian defocus blur addresses depth-of-field limitation.
* I – RGB channel swizzle is the closest to forcing luminance-only invariance.
* H – Directional motion blur simulates animal transit.

Unresolved: magnitude of depth-of-field defocus vs. fixed background asymmetry for flipping; whether channel swizzle actually improves IR robustness or just adds colour noise. Current belief: the colour→IR day→night fixed-view gap dominates, so strictly none of A-K closes it; among them horizontal flip is least harmful and most physically consistent, while Gaussian blur and channel swizzle are plausible but secondary and potentially mismatched.

The dominant domain shift is therefore spectral / colour-day → IR-night / monochrome, together with fixed background / fixed geometry vs variable GBIF scenes.

Physical constraints repeatedly cited:
* Illumination / colour is essentially locked. Brightness A/B/C, colour noise J, RGB swizzle I, and salt-and-pepper K keep or manipulate colour information that is absent at test time. Linear / non-linear brightness jitter therefore samples variation that does not exist at deployment.
* Exposure 1/500 s ~2 ms makes classic motion blur H negligible for terrestrial mammals; a directional motion-blur kernel is not a real deployment effect according to most colleagues.
* Geometry is fixed. Scale D is largely determined by species size and the small depth change along the 7 m corridor, not by free camera distance. Vertical flip E is biologically implausible.
* Depth of field at 50 mm f/4 focused at 3.5 m is only on the order of ~1-2 m total. Animals in front of / behind the focal plane will be defocused. Colleagues 10 and 5 argue this makes a Gaussian defocus blur G the only operation that simulates a real, systematic test-time effect. Others note an 11×11 σ=3 kernel is a strong, distance-independent blur and not a faithful defocus model.
* Horizontal flip F is the only colour-agnostic geometric operation that remains physically plausible: an animal can transit the pinch point left-to-right or right-to-left, giving a left-right mirror of the corridor. Several colleagues argue this is the least harmful / most useful augmentation in the list, though Colleague 1 notes mirroring also mirrors the fixed asymmetric rock background.

Competing positions:
* L None of the above. The colour → IR / day → night / variable → fixed-background shift is not bridged by any listed augmentation. Colour/brightness augmentations add variation absent at deployment, scale/blurs/flips either add unrealistic variation or do not address the spectral gap. This is the strict answer.
* F Horizontal flip. Among listed ops it is the only physically admissible, colour-agnostic regulariser that respects the fixed rig. It increases pose diversity for direction of travel without introducing modality mismatch. Repeated by Colleagues 12,15,2,6,7.
* G Gaussian blur. Defocus from limited depth of field is a systematic effect absent from sharp GBIF photos. Advocates 10,5.
* I RGB channel swizzle. Closest listed operation to forcing colour invariance / mitigating colour dependence, by destroying consistent R→R,G→G,B→B mapping and encouraging reliance on luminance/texture that is preserved under IR. Advocates 3,8. Others note it still keeps colour information and does not simulate monochrome IR.
* H Motion blur. Advocates 13,14 argue animals are still translating through the plane during exposure and GBIF data is static; opponents note 1/500 s makes translation negligible.
* D Scale augmentation. Advocate 9 argues scale mismatch between unconstrained GBIF distances and fixed 7 m baseline is first-order. Others argue scale is essentially fixed.

Unresolved / open questions: degree of left-right symmetry of the two rock faces and whether a horizontal mirror preserves the fixed background; exact depth of field and whether Gaussian blur with 11×11 σ=3 is a realistic proxy for defocus; whether any marginal gain from F outweighs the dominant spectral shift; whether forcing colour invariance via channel swizzle is better than doing nothing.

Current synthesis: No listed augmentation closes the colour-day → monochrome-IR spectral gap, which is the dominant error source. If forced to choose among the menu, the only operation that is colour-agnostic and physically plausible is a horizontal mirror, with Gaussian defocus being the only operation that simulates a real optical effect of the fixed rig. The strict, domain-correct statement remains that none of A-K materially improves deployment accuracy and real improvement requires IR/greyscale training data or explicit colour→IR domain adaptation.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: L. None of the above choices will improve deployment accuracy

The train / test gap is a fixed-geometry, fixed-photometry, spectral domain shift, not a generic natural-image shift.

* Illumination / colour. Deployment is night only, 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, under a fixed-brightness near-IR illuminator, ISO 190 f/4.0 1/500 s. The images are effectively monochrome IR with a constant overall photometric level and no useful RGB colour information. Training is several thousand GBIF multimedia images per class: daylight, visible spectrum, arbitrary white balance, exposure and background.

A,B,C,I,J,K are all RGB / photometric perturbations. Linear / non-linear brightness jitter A,B,C, RGB channel swizzle I, colour noise J and binary salt-and-pepper noise K keep colour information in the training set and teach invariance to brightness / colour variation that does not exist under a fixed IR lamp. None of them turns a colour daylight GBIF image into a monochrome fixed-IR image. Vertical flip E is biologically impossible and a horizontal flip F mirrors the fixed, non-symmetric rock corridor background. There is a real distance-dependent defocus effect, but a uniform 11×11 σ=3 Gaussian blur G is a poor, distance-independent proxy for that optics effect and adds blur that the 1/500 s shutter does not produce in the majority of the usable range. The train / test gap here is not a generic natural-image gap, it is a sensor / acquisition gap.

Deployment is a single bolted rig:
* night only, fixed-brightness near-IR illumination, ISO 190, f/4.0, 1/500 s, one frame every 30 s. Photometry is therefore essentially constant and the images are effectively monochrome / channel-redundant. There is no useful RGB colour information in the field.
* fixed viewpoint, fixed background of the two rock faces, 7 m baseline, 50 mm focal length focused at ~3.5 m. Image scale is set by species size and a very small depth range; camera pose, illumination level and sensor noise are fixed at test time.

Training is several thousand GBIF multimedia images per class:
* daylight, visible spectrum colour, arbitrary viewpoint, background, illumination and sensor.
* sharp, in-focus, colour natural-history photography.

The dominant mismatch is therefore spectral / photometric: colour daylight → fixed-brightness monochrome IR, day → night, variable background → fixed rock corridor, variable viewpoint → fixed 7 m pinch point. That shift is not closed by any of A-K.

Photometric augmentations A,B,C,I,J,K
* Linear / non-linear brightness on RGB or luminance and colour noise J, salt-and-pepper K add photometric variation that is absent at deployment because the IR illuminator + fixed ISO/f/stop/exposure lock brightness. They keep colour information in the training set and encourage reliance on colour cues that are absent at test.
* RGB channel swizzle I is the only listed operation that attacks colour dependence, but it still lives in RGB and does not simulate a monochromatic IR image. It forces a permutation invariance, not a colour→luminance collapse.

Geometric / acquisition augmentations
* Scale D creates animals at distances that can never occur at a fixed 7 m pinch point.
* Vertical flip E is biologically / physically impossible for a ground mammal in a ground-level ravine.
* Horizontal flip F is the only physically admissible left-right symmetry of a corridor camera. An animal can transit left-to-right or right-to-left and the mirror is a real deployment variation. It is colour-agnostic and does not introduce photometric variation. It is the least harmful operation in the list but it does not address the colour→IR / day→night domain shift and the GBIF set already contains left-right pose diversity.
* Gaussian blur G 11×11 σ=3 and motion blur H simulate defocus / motion that is in fact very limited here: 1/500 s makes in-exposure motion negligible for terrestrial mammals and the depth of field around 3.5 m at 50 mm f/4 is of order 1–2 m, so a strong 11×11 σ=3 blur is an over-simulation and adds a variability not dominant at test.

In strict terms the useful simulation would be a greyscale / IR conversion of the training set and freezing photometry, i.e. removing colour and brightness variation, none of which is listed. The listed augmentations either add field-inconsistent variation or keep the model tied to colour cues that will be absent at deployment and can therefore degrade deployment accuracy. If a least-harmful operation must be named from the menu, the only physically plausible, colour-agnostic geometric regulariser is the horizontal mirror F; it is still secondary to the unaddressed spectral / illumination domain shift.

F. A horizontal flip augmentation

The deployment distribution is a fixed-view, fixed-illumination, effectively monochrome IR camera trap and the training distribution is GBIF colour daylight stills with free viewpoint and background. That spectral / illumination / background gap is real and none of the listed colour/photometric ops close it.

* Illumination / colour. The rig runs 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise under a fixed-brightness IR illuminator at ISO 190, f/4.0, 1/500 s. At test time the images are effectively luminance only and brightness is practically constant. Linear / non-linear brightness A,B,C, RGB channel swizzle I, colour noise J and any RGB-based noise K therefore train the network on colour and brightness variation that does not exist at deployment and keep the model tied to colour cues that are absent in the IR stream.

* Motion / blur. 1/500 s is ~2 ms. Even a fast mammal moving a few m/s moves ≲1 cm during the exposure, i.e. negligible motion blur in the field. Directional motion blur H therefore models an artifact that is not present. A strong 11×11 σ=3 Gaussian blur G is a poor stand-in for the real distance-dependent defocus that occurs around the 3.5 m plane of best focus. Defocus is disk-shaped and varies with object distance and image position, not a globally applied uniform Gaussian, and the GBIF set already contains naturally defocused examples. Using a large uniform blur on a training set that is mostly sharp daylight photos teaches the network to expect a blur signature that is not uniformly present in the ravine.

* Scale / geometry. Camera to far rock is ~7 m, focal length 50 mm, focused at the mid-point. The nominal image scale for a given species is therefore essentially fixed by the pinch point geometry. Scale augmentation D will inject animal sizes that can never occur at this fixed baseline.

A vertical flip E is biologically impossible for terrestrial mammals in a ground-level corridor. A horizontal mirror, however, is a true symmetry of the acquisition process: the animal can transit the pinch point left-to-right or right-to-left through the same fixed viewpoint and background. The rock walls and the IR illumination are left-right symmetric to first order, so mirroring produces a physically plausible deployment instance without introducing colour, brightness, scale or blur variation that is absent at test time.

In principle the colour-day → monochrome-IR, fixed-background domain shift is not bridged by any of A-K and a grayscale/IR conversion of the training set would be required. Given the menu as written, the only colour-agnostic, physically admissible regulariser that increases effective pose diversity without adding field-inconsistent variation is a horizontal mirror. It does not close the spectral gap, but it is the least harmful and most deployment-relevant operation available.

The deployment regime is essentially fixed-geometry, fixed-photometry IR. The camera is bolted in the same place, looking 7 m down a rock corridor, ISO 190, f/4.0, 1/500 s, fixed-brightness IR illumination, night only. That means in deployment the overall brightness is essentially constant and the imagery is effectively monochrome / luminance only. The Gaussian defocus argument is appealing in principle, but the specific simulation proposed is a problem. Depth of field at 50 mm f/4 around a 3.5 m focus plane is on the order of ~1 m total, and the defocus that occurs off the plane is depth dependent and radially varying, not a fixed 11×11 σ=3 uniform blur applied to the whole image. That kernel is very aggressive for a camera trap sensor and will erase the fine pelage / texture cues that an EfficientNet B7 needs to separate 17 similar species. GBIF already contains a wide range of natural focus levels, so a strong fixed Gaussian blur is a poor proxy for the real, limited, distance-dependent defocus and introduces more train/test mismatch than it removes.

Vertical flip E is biologically impossible for terrestrial animals in a ground-level ravine.

That leaves the geometric symmetry of the corridor. Animals are funnelled through the same pinch point left-to-right and right-to-left. A left-right mirror of a physically plausible trap image is still a physically plausible trap image with the same background, illumination and camera pose, up to direction of travel. It doubles the effective pose diversity for the fixed viewpoint without introducing colour, brightness or scale variation that does not exist in deployment.

No listed augmentation closes the dominant colour-day → monochrome-IR / fixed background domain shift, so in a strict sense the gap remains. Among the options given, a horizontal mirror is the only regulariser that is colour-agnostic, physically admissible and deployment-consistent. That is why F is the most useful augmentation in the list.

Dominant domain shift is therefore spectral/photometric/background/viewpoint: colour daylight variable background → monochrome fixed-IR fixed background fixed view, day → night. Brightness is locked by fixed IR lamp + fixed ISO/f/stop/exposure, so linear/non-linear brightness A,B,C add variation that will never be seen and encourage reliance on colour cues absent at test. RGB channel swizzle I, colour noise J, salt-and-pepper K stay in RGB and keep colour dependence; none turns colour daylight into monochrome IR. Scale D is essentially fixed by the 7 m baseline and 50 mm lens; small perspective change with depth is already in GBIF, artificial rescaling teaches sizes that cannot occur.

Vertical flip E is biologically impossible for ground mammals in a ravine. Horizontal flip F is the only colour-agnostic geometric symmetry argued: an animal can transit left-to-right or right-to-left through the same pinch point. Counter-argument is that the rock background is fixed and non-symmetric, so mirroring creates a background the rig can never produce; the mirror is at best a marginal left-right direction change and it does not address the colour→IR/day→night shift. Several colleagues therefore call F the least harmful/least bad of the menu, standard camera-trap practice, but not a true bridge.

Gaussian blur G 11×11 σ=3 is offered as a defocus simulation for the limited DOF. Proponents note GBIF is sharp and deployment will have out-of-focus animals off the 3.5 m plane. Critics note the kernel is strong, uniform and distance-independent, it erases fine pelage/texture needed for 17-species classification, and the dominant error remains colour/IR/background not mild defocus. Motion blur H is argued negligible by the 1/500 s shutter; proponents of H over-estimate in-exposure translation.

Consensus after round 1: A,B,C,I,J,K are colour/brightness ops that do not close the IR gap and will encourage colour-dependent features. D is distribution-mismatched. E is unphysical. H is negligible. G captures a real optics effect but is a crude, possibly over-aggressive proxy and secondary to the spectral shift. F is the only physically admissible colour-agnostic regulariser, but it still mirrors a fixed non-symmetric background and does not close the spectral domain gap.

Unresolved: how much background asymmetry actually invalidates F; whether the modest, distance-dependent defocus is important enough to outweigh the colour shift; whether a colour-invariant proxy such as RGB swizzle I is better than a geometric mirror. Current belief leans that strictly no listed augmentation materially closes the GBIF→fixed IR trap gap and most will be neutral or harmful – i.e. L None of the above. If a forced choice from the menu is required, horizontal mirror F is the only physically plausible, colour-agnostic regulariser, with G as a distant second for optics but over-simulated.

Earlier points retained: need IR/greyscale conversion or real IR training data; fixed photometry means brightness jitter is counter-productive; fixed geometry makes scale/blur/noise augmentations introduce field-inconsistent variation.

Core argument: deployment is night fixed-brightness near-IR, effectively monochrome, constant photometry ISO 190 f/4 1/500 s, fixed viewpoint 7 m pinch point, fixed rock background. Training is GBIF daytime RGB variable viewpoint/background/illumination. Dominant gap is colour-day → monochrome-IR, day→night, variable→fixed background/viewpoint. A,B,C,I,J,K keep colour cues or add brightness variation absent at test. D scale, E vertical flip, F horizontal mirror, G Gaussian blur, H motion blur add variation absent or create physically impossible views. Real fix would be grey-scale/IR conversion or IR training data, not listed. Hence none improves.

F explicit / least-harmful: Colleagues 13,7,14 and partially 12,6,2. Argument: illumination/colour fixed, so photometric augs invalid; scale fixed; 1/500 s makes motion negligible; vertical flip impossible; horizontal mirror is the only colour-agnostic spatial symmetry of a corridor, left-right transit is physically plausible, doubles pose diversity without adding modality mismatch. Many of these authors still concede the dominant colour→IR gap is unbridged, i.e. L is strictly correct, F is only least harmful.

H motion blur bloc persists with Colleagues 13,14 from round 0, now isolated. I RGB swizzle bloc from Colleague 3 and 8 round 0 is now down to L.

Exploitable fault lines:
* IR monochrome / fixed photometry consensus now dominant; it delegitimises A,B,C,I,J,K and weakens any colour-based defence of G.
* DOF disagreement: pro-G claimed ~3–4 m DOF and systematic defocus; anti-G now argues DOF is ~1–1.2 m, defocus limited, and 11×11 σ=3 uniform Gaussian is a crude over-simulation, distance-independent, destroys texture needed for 17 species.

Claims to avoid repeating: brightness jitter helps domain adaptation; motion blur is significant at 1/500 s; scale augmentation is useful for fixed 7 m rig; Gaussian blur 11×11 σ=3 realistically simulates defocus at this optics.

reflection_text.1:
The deployment distribution is essentially fixed-geometry, fixed-photometry near-IR: camera bolted 7 m across a pinch point, 50mm lens, focused ~3.5 m mid-point, ISO 190 f/4.0 1/500 s, one frame every 30 s 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise under a fixed-brightness IR illuminator. Images are effectively monochrome/luminance with constant photometry, fixed pose, fixed rock-wall background and nominal object distance.

Training is several thousand per species GBIF multimedia: daytime visible-spectrum colour, arbitrary viewpoint, background, illumination, white balance, exposure and sensor. Dominant train-test mismatch is spectral/photometric + background/viewpoint: colour daylight → monochrome fixed-IR, day → night, variable natural background → two fixed rocks, free viewpoint → fixed 7 m optical axis. That gap is not closed by any listed A-K operation.

Photometric augmentations A,B,C,I,J,K all stay in RGB. Linear/non-linear brightness on RGB/luminance and colour noise/salt-and-pepper add brightness/colour variability that does not exist with a fixed IR lamp and keep the model learning colour cues absent at test time. RGB channel swizzle I is the only listed operation that attacks colour dependence, forcing permutation invariance and encouraging luminance/structure use, but it still lives in RGB and does not simulate a monochrome IR collapse. Brightness jitter is actively counter-productive because test brightness is fixed.

Geometry/optics. Scale D is essentially set by the 7 m baseline + 50 mm focal length + species size; the small perspective change within the corridor is already in GBIF and synthetic scale teaches sizes never seen. Vertical flip E is biologically/physically impossible for a ground mammal in a ravine. Horizontal flip F is the only colour-agnostic transform that is a true corridor symmetry: animals can transit left-to-right vs right-to-left through the same fixed viewpoint; it doubles pose diversity without adding photometric variation. It mirrors the fixed non-symmetric rock background, so it is still a modest, secondary regulariser and does not address the dominant colour→IR/day→night shift.

Motion blur H is negligible at 1/500 s ~2 ms, ≤ ~1 cm motion for terrestrial mammals. Depth of field at 50 mm f/4 focused at 3.5 m is of order ~1–2 m total, so animals off the mid-plane are defocused. Gaussian blur G with 11×11 σ=3 is a crude, distance-independent proxy for that defocus; it touches a real optics effect but the kernel is arbitrary, strong, and secondary to the spectral/background shift. Scale D, G and H therefore add variation absent at deployment or over-simulate it.

Overall consensus in round 1: no listed augmentation closes the colour/daylight → monochrome IR fixed-view domain gap; most listed ops add field-inconsistent variation or create impossible views and tend to degrade deployment accuracy. The strict answer is L. The least harmful, physically admissible regulariser in the menu is horizontal mirror F, standard camera-trap invariance, with channel swizzle I sometimes argued as the closest colour-invariance proxy and Gaussian blur G argued as the only optics-related effect present. Unresolved is how much defocus vs colour shift dominates error in practice, and whether any RGB-only operation can be net beneficial once the IR gap is acknowledged.

reflection_text.3:
The train-test mismatch is a sensor/acquisition domain shift, not generic ImageNet jitter.

Deployment is a single bolted rig: night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, fixed-brightness near-IR illuminant, ISO 190, f/4.0, 1/500 s, 50 mm lens focused at ~3.5 m mid-point of a 7 m pinch point between two rock faces, one photo every 30 s. Motion in a 1/500 s ≈2 ms exposure is ≲1 cm for terrestrial mammals, so in-exposure motion blur is negligible. Depth of field around 3.5 m at 50 mm f/4 is order ~1-1.5 m total; animals off the mid-plane will be defocused, but the effect is distance-dependent, not a uniform blur.

Training is several thousand GBIF multimedia images per species: daylight visible RGB, arbitrary viewpoint, background, illumination/white balance/exposure, sharp posed natural-history photos. Dominant failure mode is spectral/photometric/background/geometry: colour daylight variable-background variable-viewpoint → monochrome fixed-IR night fixed rock corridor fixed viewpoint.

Photometric augmentations A,B,C,I,J,K:
* Linear/non-linear brightness on RGB or luminance, RGB channel swizzle, colour noise, salt-and-pepper noise all stay in RGB and keep/encourage colour-dependent cues that are absent at test. With a fixed IR lamp brightness variation does not exist at deployment, so brightness jitter adds non-existent variation.
* RGB channel swizzle I is the only listed operation that attacks colour dependence; it forces permutation invariance but still lives in RGB and does not produce greyscale/IR.
* None of A-K is a grey-scale/IR conversion, which is what would actually close the colour→IR day→night gap.

Geometric/acquisition augmentations:
* Scale D: image scale is set by the 7 m baseline and 50 mm focal length; only a small perspective change with depth remains. Scale jitter teaches sizes that will never occur.
* Vertical flip E is biologically/physically impossible for a ground mammal in a ground-level ravine.
* Horizontal flip F: animals can transit left-to-right or right-to-left through the same corridor, so a left-right mirror is a physically plausible, colour-agnostic symmetry. It mirrors a fixed non-symmetric rock background, but it is the only colour-agnostic transformation that does not introduce photometric variation absent at test. Most colleagues treat F as the least harmful/standard camera-trap invariance, but it does not address the dominant colour→IR/background shift.
* Gaussian blur G 11×11 σ=3: a real defocus effect exists off the 3.5 m plane, and colleagues 10,5 argue this is the only listed augmentation that mimics a real optics effect present at deployment. Counter-argument: the kernel is strong, uniform and distance-independent, not a realistic PSF, and the dominant error is spectral/background not mild defocus.
* Motion blur H: argued by colleagues 13,14 as dominant because animals are moving, but 1/500 s makes directional smear negligible for terrestrial mammals; the claimed effect is not supported by the exposure.

Strictly, none of A-K bridges the colour-day → monochrome-IR night, variable background → fixed rock corridor, variable viewpoint → fixed 7 m viewpoint shift. The useful operation would be desaturate/greyscale/IR-simulate training data and/or train on real IR camera-trap data, which is not listed. Hence L = none of the above will improve deployment accuracy is the technically correct statement on the menu as written.

If a least-harmful choice must be forced, the consensus least-harmful is F horizontal flip as the only physically admissible colour-agnostic geometric regulariser; G Gaussian defocus and I RGB swizzle are the next most commonly defended proxies for optics and colour invariance, but both remain secondary to the unbridged spectral domain gap.

Unresolved: exact sensor size → precise depth of field and pixel scale; whether the IR sensor returns true monochrome or three redundant channels; degree of left-right asymmetry of the rock corridor that would make a horizontal mirror unrealistic; whether the model would actually benefit from a defocus simulation versus relying on GBIF natural focus diversity.

If a choice must be forced from the menu, the only deployment-consistent, colour-agnostic regulariser is horizontal flip F, with Gaussian defocus G being the only optics-motivated argument. reflection_text.4:
The deployment is a fixed-pose night IR camera trap: camera bolted at one rock face looking ~7 m down the pinch point to the opposite rock, 50 mm focal length, focused at ~3.5 m mid-point, ISO 190, f/4.0, 1/500 s, fixed-brightness IR illumination, photos 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise every 30 s. Deployment images are effectively monochrome IR with essentially constant photometry, fixed background, fixed viewpoint and essentially fixed image scale for a given species.

Training data is GBIF multimedia: daytime, visible-spectrum colour, highly variable viewpoint, background, illumination, exposure and scale. Dominant domain shift is spectral / colour-day → IR-night / monochrome, together with fixed background / fixed geometry vs variable GBIF scenes.

Physical constraints repeatedly cited:
* Illumination / colour is essentially locked. Brightness A/B/C, colour noise J, RGB swizzle I, and salt-and-pepper K keep or manipulate colour information that is absent at test time. Linear / non-linear brightness jitter therefore samples variation that does not exist at deployment.
* Exposure 1/500 s ~2 ms makes classic motion blur H negligible for terrestrial mammals; a directional motion-blur kernel is not a real deployment effect according to most colleagues.
* Geometry is fixed. Scale D is largely determined by species size and the small depth change along the 7 m corridor, not by free camera distance. Vertical flip E is biologically implausible.
* Depth of field at 50 mm f/4 focused at 3.5 m is only on the order of ~1-2 m total. Animals in front of / behind the focal plane will be defocused. Colleagues 10 and 5 argue this makes a Gaussian defocus blur G the only operation that simulates a real, systematic test-time effect. Others note an 11×11 σ=3 kernel is a strong, distance-independent blur and not a faithful defocus model.
* Horizontal flip F is the only colour-agnostic geometric operation that remains physically plausible: an animal can transit the pinch point left-to-right or right-to-left, giving a left-right mirror of the corridor. Several colleagues argue this is the least harmful / most useful augmentation in the list, though Colleague 1 notes mirroring also mirrors the fixed asymmetric rock background.

Competing positions after round 1:
* L None of the above. The colour → IR / day → night / variable → fixed-background shift is not bridged by any listed augmentation. Colour/brightness augmentations add variation absent at deployment, scale/blurs/flips either add unrealistic variation or do not address the spectral gap. This is the strict answer, repeatedly made by Colleagues 1,10,11,2,4,5,6,8,9.
* F Horizontal flip. Among listed ops it is the only physically admissible, colour-agnostic regulariser that respects the fixed rig. It increases pose diversity for direction of travel without introducing modality mismatch. Repeated by Colleagues 12,13,14,15,7,6.
* G Gaussian blur. Defocus from limited depth of field is a systematic effect absent from sharp GBIF photos. Advocates 10,5. Opponents say 11×11 σ=3 is too strong and distance-independent.
* I RGB channel swizzle. Closest listed operation to forcing colour invariance / mitigating colour dependence, by destroying consistent R→R,G→G,B→B mapping and encouraging reliance on luminance/texture that is preserved under IR. Advocates 3,8. Others note it still keeps colour information and does not simulate monochrome IR.
* H Motion blur. Advocates 13,14 argue animals are still translating through the plane during exposure and GBIF data is static; opponents note 1/500 s makes translation negligible.
* D Scale augmentation. Advocate 9 argues scale mismatch between unconstrained GBIF distances and fixed 7 m baseline is first-order. Others argue scale is essentially fixed.

Unresolved / open questions: degree of left-right symmetry of the two rock faces and whether a horizontal mirror preserves the fixed background; exact depth of field and whether Gaussian blur with 11×11 σ=3 is a realistic proxy for defocus; whether any marginal gain from F outweighs the dominant spectral shift; whether forcing colour invariance via channel swizzle is better than doing nothing.

Current synthesis: No listed augmentation closes the colour-day → monochrome-IR spectral gap, which is the dominant error source. If forced to choose among the menu, the only operation that is colour-agnostic and physically plausible is a horizontal mirror, with Gaussian defocus being the only operation that simulates a real optical effect of the fixed rig. The strict, domain-correct statement remains that none of A-K materially improves deployment accuracy and real improvement requires IR/greyscale training data or explicit colour→IR domain adaptation.
reflection_text.5:
The deployment distribution is tightly constrained and very different from GBIF training.

Deployment facts repeatedly emphasized:
* Night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, fixed-brightness near-IR illumination, ISO 190, f/4.0, 1/500 s, camera bolted at one rock face looking 7 m to the other, 50 mm focal length focused at ~3.5 m midpoint. Images are effectively monochrome/luminance-only with practically constant photometry. Background = two rock faces, pose, nominal object distance and illumination level are constant.
* 1/500 s ≈2 ms → in-exposure motion ≲1 cm for terrestrial mammals, so directional motion blur is negligible in the field.
* Depth of field at 50 mm f/4 around 3.5 m is ~1-2 m total. Real defocus exists for animals off the mid-plane, but it is distance-dependent and limited.

Training facts:
* Several thousand GBIF multimedia images per species per class, daytime visible-spectrum RGB, arbitrary viewpoint, background, illumination, white balance, exposure.
* Dominant failure mode = spectral/photometric: colour daylight variable background free viewpoint → monochrome fixed-IR fixed background fixed viewpoint, plus day→night.

Augmentation analysis converging:
* Photometric A,B,C,I,J,K: linear/non-linear brightness on RGB/luminance, RGB channel swizzle, colour noise, salt-and-pepper. All keep colour information in training and/or add brightness/colour variation that does not exist with fixed IR lamp. They encourage colour-dependent cues that are absent at test and are counter-productive. No listed operation does a grey-scale/IR conversion.
* Scale D: image scale is essentially set by the 7 m baseline + 50 mm lens + species size; small perspective change with depth is already in GBIF. Synthetic scale teaches sizes that will never occur.
* Vertical flip E: universally deemed biologically/physically impossible for ground mammals in a ground-level ravine.
* Motion blur H: negligible at 1/500 s; most colleagues now reject the fast-mover argument.
* Gaussian blur G 11×11 σ=3: only optics-related effect in list. Defocus does exist, but the prescribed kernel is uniform, strong and distance-independent; a poor proxy for the narrow, distance-dependent defocus around 3.5 m and secondary to the colour→IR shift.
* Horizontal flip F: animals can transit left-to-right or right-to-left through the pinch point. It is colour-agnostic and does not add photometric variation. Several colleagues argue it is still mirroring a fixed non-symmetric rock background and does not address the dominant spectral/background shift; others argue it is the only physically admissible geometric regulariser and standard camera-trap invariance.

Consensus points from round 1 and reinforced in round 0 current:
* Colour/brightness jitter does not bridge day colour → night IR; fixed illumination means brightness variation is spurious.
* Motion blur is unlikely; vertical flip implausible.
* Real improvement would require IR/greyscale training data or domain adaptation, which is not listed.

Disagreement remains on least-worst listed augmentation:
* L – None improves deployment accuracy; all listed augmentations are neutral/harmful and the gap is unbridgeable by A-K.
* F – Horizontal flip is the only physically plausible, colour-agnostic regulariser and the least harmful.
* G – Gaussian defocus blur addresses depth-of-field limitation, though kernel is mismatched.
* I – RGB channel swizzle is closest to forcing luminance-only invariance; this argument is now minority and largely superseded by L/F positions.

Current belief: Strictly, the dominant colour/day → monochrome/IR fixed-view fixed-background shift is not closed by any A-K operation, so the correct statement on the menu is L. Among the listed options, horizontal flip F is the least harmful, physically admissible geometric symmetry and the standard camera-trap invariance, while Gaussian blur and channel swizzle are secondary and potentially mismatched. Unresolved is whether an exam expects the strict L answer or the least-harmful F interpretation.
reflection_text.12:
The train / test gap is a sensor / acquisition domain shift, not a generic ImageNet robustness gap.

Deployment
* Single bolted rig: 7 m baseline rock-to-rock, 50 mm lens, focused ~3.5 m mid-point, f/4.0, ISO 190, 1/500 s, one frame /30 s, 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise under a fixed-brightness near-IR illuminator.
* Images are effectively monochrome / luminance-only IR with practically constant photometry, fixed camera pose, fixed rock-wall background, and nominal object distance essentially fixed. Scale is set by species size + small depth change in the pinch point. 1/500 s ≈2 ms → in-exposure translation is cm-scale, motion blur negligible. Depth of field around 3.5 m at 50 mm f/4 is ~1–2 m total, so modest distance-dependent defocus exists off the plane of best focus.

Training
* Several thousand GBIF multimedia images / class: daytime visible-spectrum RGB, arbitrary viewpoint, background, illumination, white balance, exposure. Sharp natural-history photos.

Dominant mismatch
* Spectral / photometric: colour daylight → fixed-brightness monochrome IR, day → night.
* Background / viewpoint: variable natural background and free viewpoint → fixed rock corridor and fixed 7 m viewpoint.
* The colour→IR / day→night shift is the primary failure mode.

Why the listed augmentations do not close it
* A,B,C linear / non-linear brightness, I RGB channel swizzle, J colour noise, K salt-and-pepper: all RGB / photometric ops. They keep colour information in training and/or add brightness / colour variability that does not exist with a fixed IR lamp. They encourage reliance on colour cues absent at test. Brightness jitter is counter-productive.
* D scale: image scale is essentially fixed by the 7 m baseline and 50 mm lens; synthetic scale teaches invariance to sizes that will never occur.
* E vertical flip: biologically / physically impossible for a ground mammal in a ground-level ravine.
* H motion blur: 1/500 s makes directional motion blur negligible for terrestrial mammals.
* G Gaussian blur 11×11 σ=3: defocus is real off the 3.5 m plane, but the listed kernel is a strong, distance-independent proxy, not the true depth-dependent PSF, and it is secondary to the spectral shift.
* F horizontal flip: the only colour-agnostic transform that is physically plausible for a corridor; animals can transit left-to-right or right-to-left. It mirrors the fixed, non-symmetric rock background but does not introduce photometric variation. It is the least harmful / standard camera-trap invariance, but it does not address colour→IR / day→night.

Channel swizzle I is the only listed op that attacks colour dependence, pushing the network toward luminance / texture cues, but it remains RGB and does not simulate a monochromatic IR image. Several colleagues argue it is the closest proxy to needed colour→IR invariance; others argue it still keeps colour in the loop.

Consensus in the current round
* Strictly, none of A-K converts RGB daylight GBIF data into fixed-brightness monochrome IR fixed-view fixed-background data. The useful operation would be grey-scale / IR conversion and photometry freezing, which is not listed.
* Hence in strict terms L, none of the above, is correct; most listed augmentations add field-inconsistent variation and can degrade performance.
* If forced to pick the least harmful from the menu, the discussion converges on F horizontal mirror as the only physically admissible, colour-agnostic geometric regulariser, with a secondary argument for G as a coarse proxy for limited DOF and for I as the best attempt to reduce colour dependence.

Unresolved: how much weight to give the secondary defocus effect vs the primary spectral shift. Current belief: L is the defensible scientific answer; F is the best practical choice among the given options, with I and G as the next most discussed but still insufficient.
reflection_text.9:
The deployment distribution is essentially fixed-geometry, fixed-photometry near-IR and the training distribution is GBIF daylight RGB.

Acquisition facts retained: camera bolted at one rock face looking 7 m to the other, 50 mm focal length, focus at ~3.5 m mid-point, ISO 190, f/4.0, 1/500 s, fixed-brightness IR illuminator, night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, 1 frame/30 s. Training is GBIF multimedia: daytime, visible RGB, arbitrary viewpoint/background/illumination/exposure.

Dominant mismatch is spectral/illumination + background/viewpoint. Deployment images are effectively monochrome IR with practically constant brightness; training is colour daylight with variable photometry. Brightness A/B/C, colour noise J, RGB swizzle I, colour-dependent tone curve C all stay in the RGB colour domain and do not create a colour→IR/greyscale transfer. They also introduce variation in brightness/noise that is essentially absent at test time.

Geometry: scale, pose and background are essentially fixed by the 7 m pinch point and the rock walls. Scale D adds variation that will not occur. Vertical flip E is biologically/physically impossible. Horizontal flip F is the only geometric symmetry that is physically plausible for a corridor – an animal can transit left-to-right or right-to-left through the same fixed view – and is the standard camera-trap invariance. It does not close the colour→IR gap, and several colleagues note the fixed non-symmetric rock background makes even F create views the camera cannot produce.

Optics arguments:
* Motion blur H is negligible at 1/500 s for terrestrial mammals; estimated motion ≤~1 cm during exposure. Colleagues 13/14 argue directional motion exists, majority argue it is negligible.
* Depth of field at 50 mm f/4 focused ~3.5 m is ~ a few metres, about ~1 m total around the focus plane. Animals in front/behind the mid-plane will be defocused. Colleagues 10/5 argue Gaussian defocus blur G is the only listed effect that matches a real deployment variation; colleagues 12/6/7/14 note the 11×11 σ=3 kernel is a strong, distance-independent approximation and the colour→IR shift dominates anyway.
* Scale D is constrained by the fixed baseline; the small perspective change with depth is already covered in GBIF.

Colour invariance arguments: Channel swizzle I and, to a lesser extent, horizontal flip F are the only listed operations that are colour-agnostic and could reduce reliance on RGB cues. Swizzle forces luminance/structure reliance, but still keeps three-channel colour information and does not simulate monochromatic IR. No listed augmentation actually desaturates/greyscales the training set.

Disagreement captured in round 1:
L camp: 1,10,11,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 argue none of A-K closes the day-colour→night-IR, fixed-background, fixed-view domain shift; most augmentations add field-inconsistent variation.
F camp: 12,13,14,15,7,2,6 argue horizontal mirror is the only physically admissible, least harmful augmentation in the menu.
G camp: 10,5 argue defocus Gaussian blur is the only real optics mismatch.
H camp: 13,14 argue directional motion blur is key sharp-vs-moving mismatch.
I camp: 3,8 argue RGB channel swizzle is closest to forcing colour invariance.
D camp: 9 argues scale mismatch is dominant geometric shift.

Current belief: The colour→monochrome IR, day→night, fixed-view domain shift is not bridged by any listed augmentation. In a strict sense L is correct and the listed augmentations are neutral or harmful. If forced to pick the least harmful / most deployment-relevant operation among the menu, horizontal flip F is the only physically plausible, colour-agnostic regulariser; Gaussian blur G captures the depth-of-field defocus that is real but is a coarse proxy and still secondary to the spectral shift. Unresolved is whether the rock background asymmetry makes even F unrealistic, and whether the listed 11×11 σ=3 blur is a reasonable defocus model for the ~3.5 m focus plane. The needed operation is explicit greyscale/IR conversion / IR-matched training data, which is not listed.
reflection_text.11:
The deployment domain is a fixed-geometry, fixed-photometry near-IR night trap: camera bolted at one rock face looking 7 m to opposite rock, 50 mm focal length, focused at ~3.5 m mid-point, ISO 190, f/4.0, 1/500 s, fixed-brightness IR illuminator, 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, 1 photo/30 s. Images are effectively monochrome/luminance-only with essentially constant brightness, constant rock corridor background, and very narrow depth/scale range set by the 7 m baseline.

Training domain is GBIF multimedia scraped for ~17 species, several thousand images per species: daylight visible RGB, unconstrained viewpoint, illumination, background, camera and distance. Dominant shift is colour daylight → monochrome IR night, variable background → fixed rock corridor, variable viewpoint/scale → fixed viewpoint/scale.

Key claims held across rounds:
* Illumination / colour: fixed IR means no meaningful brightness/colour variation at test. Linear/non-linear brightness A,B,C, colour noise J, RGB swizzle I, salt-and-pepper K all keep colour information and add variation absent at deployment; they encourage reliance on colour cues absent at test. Brightness jitter is actively counter-productive because test brightness is locked.
* Geometry: scale is essentially fixed by 7 m pinch point and 50 mm lens; small scale change is due to depth in front of/behind focus plane. Depth of field at 50 mm f/4 focused at 3.5 m is of order ~1–4 m total, so animals off mid-plane will be defocused. Supports defocus argument for Gaussian blur G. 1/500 s ~2 ms, so motion blur H is negligible for typical terrestrial mammals, ~≤1 cm motion per exposure.
* Orientation: vertical flip E is biologically/physically impossible for ground mammals in a corridor. Horizontal mirror F corresponds to left-to-right vs right-to-left transit through the same fixed corridor and is the only colour-agnostic spatial symmetry in the list; several colleagues note the rock background is non-symmetric so mirroring creates a background the rig cannot produce, others treat corridor as left-right symmetric to first order.
* Colour invariance: RGB channel swizzle I destroys fixed R/G/B mapping and forces reliance on luminance/texture, closest listed operation to attacking colour→IR shift, but still leaves colour statistics and does not create grey-scale/IR.
* Scale D increases/decreases resolution; with fixed rig this introduces scale variation absent at test.
* Motion blur H argued by some as relevant for moving animals; countered by 1/500 s physics and fixed shutter.
* Gaussian blur G 11×11 σ=3 is a crude, distance-independent proxy for depth-of-field defocus; real defocus is distance-dependent and radially varying, and a strong uniform blur can erase fine pelage cues. Defocus is real but secondary to spectral/background shift.

Current deliberation consensus:
Majority of colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 assert L: none of A-K materially closes GBIF→IR trap gap, most augmentations add field-inconsistent variation or create physically impossible views and tend to degrade deployment accuracy. Real improvement requires grey-scale/IR conversion / IR training data or explicit colour→IR domain adaptation, not listed.
Minority 13,14,7 argue F horizontal flip is the only physically admissible, colour-agnostic regulariser that respects corridor geometry and increases effective pose diversity without introducing modality mismatch; they accept spectral gap remains unbridged.
Earlier minority positions for G Gaussian blur as defocus simulation, I RGB channel swizzle as colour-invariance proxy, and H motion blur are now largely rejected given 1/500 s and fixed illumination.

Unresolved: exact sensor size for DOF calculation and how much depth variation is actually encountered in practice; whether 11×11 σ=3 is a reasonable defocus proxy; degree of left-right asymmetry of the fixed rock background.

My current belief: strictly speaking the dominant failure mode is spectral/illumination/background domain shift which no listed augmentation closes; correct strict answer is L. If forced to pick a least-harmful, deployment-consistent operation from the menu, horizontal flip F is the only colour-agnostic, physically plausible symmetry, with Gaussian blur G being the strongest optics-based argument for a real but secondary effect. Brightness/colour/scale/noise augmentations are counter-productive.
reflection_text.10:
The deployment domain is a fixed-pose, fixed-photometry night IR camera trap: camera 7 m across a pinch point, 50 mm lens, focused at ~3.5 m mid-point, ISO 190 f/4.0 1/500 s, fixed-brightness IR illuminator, night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, 30 s cadence. Training domain is GBIF multimedia: daylight RGB, unconstrained viewpoint, background, illumination, sensor.

Dominant mismatch is spectral/illumination/background. Training is colour daylight with variable background/pose; test is effectively monochrome fixed-brightness IR with a single rock-corridor background and fixed camera pose. Brightness is essentially constant at deployment, so linear/non-linear brightness A/B/C, colour noise J, RGB swizzle I, black-white noise K do not simulate IR and can encourage reliance on colour cues absent at test. ISO 190 f/4 1/500 s is low noise, so sensor noise augmentations are unrealistic.

Geometry is also constrained. Scale is essentially fixed by the 7 m baseline and 50 mm focal length; only small depth variation along the corridor. DOF around the 3.5 m focus plane at 50 mm f/4 is of order ~1–2 m total, so animals off the mid-plane will be defocused. Colleagues 10,5 argue this is the only real physical variation captured by Gaussian blur G 11×11 σ=3. Colleagues 1,11,4,6,14 note the kernel is a crude, distance-independent, overly strong stand-in for a small, depth-dependent defocus and is secondary to the colour→IR shift.

Orientation: vertical flip E is biologically implausible. Horizontal flip F is physically plausible for a corridor: animals can transit left-to-right or right-to-left through the same fixed viewpoint. Colleagues 12,2,6,7,13,14,15 make F the “least harmful / most deployment-consistent” geometric regulariser, while colleagues 1,11,4,8,9 note even F mirrors a fixed asymmetric rock background and does not address the dominant domain shift. Some now explicitly state the mirror creates a background the rig can never produce.

Colour invariance arguments: Colleagues 3,8 argue RGB channel swizzle I is the only listed operation that attacks colour dependence and forces reliance on luminance/structure preserved under IR, making it the closest proxy for a grey-scale/IR conversion. Others argue swizzle keeps colour information in training and does not create monochrome IR statistics.

Motion blur H is negligible at 1/500 s for terrestrial mammals ~≤1 cm motion during exposure; several colleagues state directional smear is not a real deployment effect. Scale augmentation D creates animals at distances that cannot occur at a fixed 7 m pinch point.

Overall disagreement persists:
- Strict view: none of A-K closes the colour/day → IR/night, fixed-viewpoint gap; most augmentations add variation absent at deployment or create physically impossible views → L. This is the position of colleagues 1,10,11,12,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,15.
- Pragmatic “best among bad” view: horizontal mirror F is the only colour-agnostic, physically admissible transformation for the fixed corridor. Colleagues 12,2,6,7,13,14,15 hold this.
- Defocus view: Gaussian blur G simulates DOF-limited defocus from front/back of the ravine. Colleagues 10,5.
- Colour-invariance view: RGB channel swizzle I best mitigates colour dependence. Colleagues 3,8.

Unresolved: whether DOF defocus or left-right symmetry dominates over the unbridgeable spectral shift; whether mirroring a fixed rock background is truly deployment-consistent. No listed augmentation provides grey-scale/IR conversion, which would be required to truly bridge the GBIF → IR gap. Current best synthesis is that strictly none improve deployment accuracy, with horizontal flip being the least harmful physically plausible augmentation if forced to choose from the menu, and RGB swizzle being the only operation that even attempts colour invariance.
reflection_text.15:
The deployment is a single fixed rig: 7 m rock-to-rock pinch point, 50 mm lens focused at ~3.5 m, ISO 190 f/4.0 1/500 s, night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise with fixed-brightness near-IR illumination. Images are effectively monochrome IR, constant photometry, fixed pose, fixed rock-wall background, fixed nominal scale for a given species. The 1/500 s exposure ≈2 ms gives ≤~1 cm in-exposure translation for terrestrial mammals, so directional motion blur H is negligible. Depth of field around 3.5 m at 50 mm f/4 is order ~1 m total, so a real distance-dependent defocus exists for animals off the mid-plane, but it is limited.

Training is several thousand GBIF multimedia images per class: daytime visible RGB, arbitrary viewpoint, background, illumination, white balance, exposure, sharp natural-history photography.

Dominant domain shift is therefore spectral/photometric/background/viewpoint: colour daylight variable background → monochrome fixed-IR fixed background fixed view, day → night. Brightness is locked by fixed IR lamp + fixed ISO/f/stop/exposure, so linear/non-linear brightness A,B,C add variation that will never be seen and encourage reliance on colour cues absent at test. RGB channel swizzle I, colour noise J, salt-and-pepper K stay in RGB and keep colour dependence; none turns colour daylight into monochrome IR. Scale D is essentially fixed by the 7 m baseline and 50 mm lens; small perspective change with depth is already in GBIF, artificial rescaling teaches sizes that cannot occur.

Vertical flip E is biologically impossible for ground mammals in a ravine. Horizontal flip F is the only colour-agnostic geometric symmetry argued: an animal can transit left-to-right or right-to-left through the same pinch point. Counter-argument is that the rock background is fixed and non-symmetric, so mirroring creates a background the rig can never produce; the mirror is at best a marginal left-right direction change and it does not address the colour→IR/day→night shift. Several colleagues therefore call F the least harmful/least bad of the menu, standard camera-trap practice, but not a true bridge.

Gaussian blur G 11×11 σ=3 is offered as a defocus simulation for the limited DOF. Proponents note GBIF is sharp and deployment will have out-of-focus animals off the 3.5 m plane. Critics note the kernel is strong, uniform and distance-independent, it erases fine pelage/texture needed for 17-species classification, and the dominant error remains colour/IR/background not mild defocus. Motion blur H is argued negligible by the 1/500 s shutter; proponents of H over-estimate in-exposure translation.

Consensus after round 1: A,B,C,I,J,K are colour/brightness ops that do not close the IR gap and will encourage colour-dependent features. D is distribution-mismatched. E is unphysical. H is negligible. G captures a real optics effect but is a crude, possibly over-aggressive proxy and secondary to the spectral shift. F is the only physically admissible colour-agnostic regulariser, but it still mirrors a fixed non-symmetric background and does not close the spectral domain gap.

Unresolved: how much background asymmetry actually invalidates F; whether the modest, distance-dependent defocus is important enough to outweigh the colour shift; whether a colour-invariant proxy such as RGB swizzle I is better than a geometric mirror. Current belief leans that strictly no listed augmentation materially closes the GBIF→fixed IR trap gap and most will be neutral or harmful – i.e. L None of the above. If a forced choice from the menu is required, horizontal mirror F is the only physically plausible, colour-agnostic regulariser, with G as a distant second for optics but over-simulated.

Earlier points retained: need IR/greyscale conversion or real IR training data; fixed photometry means brightness jitter is counter-productive; fixed geometry makes scale/blur/noise augmentations introduce field-inconsistent variation.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: L. None of the above choices will materially improve deployment accuracy on the menu as written.

The train / test gap is a sensor / acquisition domain shift, not a generic ImageNet-style robustness gap.

Deployment is a single bolted rig: night only 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, fixed-brightness near-IR illuminator, ISO 190, f/4.0, 1/500 s, 50 mm focal length focused at ~3.5 m mid-point of a 7 m pinch point. Images are effectively monochrome / luminance-only, photometrically essentially constant, fixed viewpoint, fixed rock-wall background, fixed nominal object distance and fixed scale for a given species. 1/500 s ≈2 ms makes in-exposure motion blur negligible for terrestrial mammals, ≲1 cm.

Training is several thousand GBIF multimedia images per species: daytime visible RGB, arbitrary viewpoint, background, illumination / white balance / exposure, sharp natural-history photography.

The dominant failure mode is therefore spectral / photometric / background / geometry: colour daylight variable-background variable-viewpoint → monochrome fixed-IR night fixed rock corridor fixed viewpoint.

A,B,C,I,J,K are all RGB colour-space operations. Linear / non-linear brightness on RGB or luminance, RGB channel swizzle, colour noise, salt-and-pepper noise keep colour information in the training set and encourage colour dependent cues that are absent at test. With a fixed IR lamp brightness variation does not exist at deployment, so brightness jitter adds non-existent variation. None of them performs a colour→greyscale / IR conversion that would be required to close the day→night spectral shift.

D scale is essentially fixed by the 7 m baseline and 50 mm lens; the residual perspective change with depth is small and GBIF already spans a much wider scale distribution. E vertical flip is biologically impossible for a ground mammal in a ravine. F horizontal flip is the only colour-agnostic symmetry in the list and an animal can transit left-to-right or right-to-left, but it mirrors the fixed non-symmetric rock background and, crucially, it does not address the colour→IR / day→night / variable→fixed background domain shift that dominates error. It is the least harmful operation in the set, not an improving one.

G Gaussian blur 11×11 σ=3 is a crude distance-independent proxy for defocus. Real defocus in the field is distance-dependent around the 3.5 m plane of best focus at 50 mm f/4 and the depth of field is ~1-1.5 m total. H motion blur is negligible at 1/500 s for terrestrial mammals.

The operation that would actually close the gap is a greyscale / IR simulation of the training data and matching to the fixed IR photometry / fixed background / fixed viewpoint, i.e. training on IR-representative camera-trap data. That operation is not listed in A-K.

With the menu as written the listed photometric and geometric perturbations either add variation that is absent at deployment, create physically impossible views, or preserve colour dependence that is destroyed by IR. They do not bridge the GBIF → fixed IR trap gap and will tend to be neutral to degrading. Strictly, none of A-K materially improves deployment accuracy.

Deployment is a single bolted rig: night only, 30 min after sundown to 30 min before sunrise, fixed-brightness near-IR illuminator, ISO 190, f/4.0, 1/500 s, 50 mm lens focused at ~3.5 m looking 7 m down a rock pinch point. The images seen in the field are effectively monochrome / luminance only, with practically constant photometry, a fixed camera pose, a fixed two-rock background and a fixed nominal object distance. Sensor noise and motion during the ~2 ms exposure are negligible.

Training is several thousand GBIF multimedia images per class: daytime visible-spectrum RGB, arbitrary viewpoint, background, illumination, white balance and exposure. The dominant failure mode is therefore colour-daylight variable-background variable-viewpoint → monochrome fixed-IR night fixed-background fixed-viewpoint. That spectral / photometric / background shift is not addressed by any listed augmentation.

A,B,C,I,J,K are all RGB / photometric operations. Linear / non-linear brightness on RGB or luminance, colour noise, salt-and-pepper noise and RGB channel swizzle keep colour information in the training set and actively encourage the EfficientNet B7 to learn colour dependent cues that are absent at test time. With a fixed IR lamp brightness variation does not exist at deployment, so brightness/tone jitter adds variation that will never be seen and makes the model rely on photometry that is constant in the field.

D scale augmentation teaches scale invariance to a variation that is essentially locked by the 7 m baseline and 50 mm focal length. E vertical flip is biologically impossible for a ground mammal in a ravine. F a horizontal mirror is the only colour-agnostic spatial symmetry in the list and is the standard camera-trap invariance, but it still mirrors the fixed non-symmetric rock background and, crucially, it does not touch the colour→IR day→night domain shift that dominates error. It is at best the least harmful option, not a performance gain.

H motion blur is negligible at 1/500 s for terrestrial mammals in a narrow funnel. G a fixed 11×11 σ=3 Gaussian blur is a uniform, distance-independent proxy for defocus. Real defocus in this rig is depth-dependent and limited to the ~1 m depth of field around the 3.5 m plane of focus, and the dominant systematic error remains the spectral / background / day-night shift. A strong global Gaussian adds blur variability that the fixed rig does not have in deployment and will erode the fine pelage / texture cues needed to separate 17 similar species under IR.

In practice the operation that would materially help is a grey-scale / IR conversion of the training data and matching to the fixed IR statistics, i.e. training on IR representative data with the fixed background and photometry. That operation is not in A-K. With the menu as written the listed photometric and geometric perturbations either add field-inconsistent variation, create physically impossible views, or preserve the colour dependence that is destroyed by IR. Strictly, none of the offered augmentations materially improves, and most will tend to degrade, deployment accuracy for the GBIF → fixed IR camera-trap transfer.

The deployment distribution is a single fixed-sensor, fixed-scene regime and the GBIF training distribution is the exact opposite of it, so the listed augmentations do not close the gap that matters.

Deployment is night only, 30 min after sundundown to 30 min before sunrise, under a fixed-brightness near-IR illuminator, ISO 190, f/4.0, 1/500 s, one bolted rig looking 7 m down the pinch point at the opposite rock wall, focused at ~3.5 m. Photometry is essentially constant and the signal is effectively monochrome / luminance only. Viewpoint, background, nominal object distance and illumination geometry are all locked for the whole field season. Scale for a given species is set by the 7 m baseline and 50 mm focal length; the only residual depth change is the ~1 m usable depth of field around the focus plane.

Training is several thousand GBIF multimedia images per class: daytime visible RGB, arbitrary viewpoint, background, white balance and exposure. The dominant failure mode is therefore spectral / photometric / background: colour daylight variable background variable viewpoint → monochrome fixed-IR night fixed rock corridor fixed viewpoint. That is the error that will dominate EfficientNet B7 performance on the 17 species.

A,B,C,I,J,K are all RGB / photometric operations. Linear / non-linear brightness on RGB or luminance, RGB channel swizzle, colour noise and salt-and-pepper noise keep colour information in the training set and encourage reliance on colour cues that are absent in the IR stream. With a fixed IR lamp brightness jitter does not exist at test time, so A,B,C add variation that will never be seen and that actively harms the fixed-photometry prior.

Scale D, vertical flip E and even horizontal flip F are geometric. The rig is bolted; image scale is fixed by geometry. A vertical flip is biologically impossible for a ground mammal in a ravine. A horizontal mirror is the only colour-agnostic symmetry in the list, but it mirrors the fixed, non-symmetric rock background and rig orientation that the camera will actually see. It does not address the colour → IR / day → night shift and it creates training examples of a background that cannot be produced by the camera.

Motion blur H is negligible at 1/500 s for terrestrial mammals, ~cm of motion in the exposure. The only real optics effect present off the plane of best focus is distance-dependent defocus. The menu’s Gaussian blur G is a uniform 11×11 σ=3 kernel applied independent of object distance. That is a crude, distance-independent proxy that is much stronger than the modest ~1 m depth of field at 50 mm f/4 around 3.5 m and it destroys the fine pelage / texture cues needed to separate 17 similar species in monochrome IR. More importantly, even a perfect defocus model would not turn colour daylight GBIF photos into fixed-brightness monochrome IR with a fixed rock corridor background.

What would actually help is a grey-scale / IR conversion of the training set and matching to the fixed IR statistics, i.e. training on IR representative data. That operation is not in A–K. With the menu as written the augmentations either add field-inconsistent variation, create physically impossible views, or preserve the colour dependence that is destroyed by IR. In strict terms none of A-K materially improves, and most tend to degrade, deployment accuracy for the GBIF → fixed IR camera-trap transfer.
